authors: Hefei Wen, Jason M. Hockenberry, Janet R. Cummings
title: The effect of Medicaid expansion on crime reduction: Evidence from HIFA-waiver expansions
key_finding: Early public-insurance expansions generated significant reductions in arrests, with effects concentrated in property and violent categories; treatment access acts through substitution away from criminal-justice contact toward care.
relevance_to_our_pattern: Direct precedent: pre-ACA public MH/health spending expansions causally reduce crime.

authors: Jacob Vogler
title: Access to Health Care and Criminal Behavior: Short-Run Evidence from the ACA Medicaid Expansions
venue: Journal of Policy Analysis and Management
key_finding: States that expanded Medicaid experienced a 5.3% reduction in annual reported violent crime, explained by decreases in aggravated assault; effect tied to insurance-eligibility gains.
relevance_to_our_pattern: The 14-expansion test: same sign as our MO-DMH lane (-).

authors: Qiwei He, Scott Barkowski
title: The effect of health insurance on crime: Evidence from the Affordable Care Act Medicaid expansion
key_finding: ACA Medicaid expansion was negatively associated with burglary, vehicle theft, homicide, robbery, and assault; availability of coverage raises the opportunity cost of crime.
relevance_to_our_pattern: Strongest direct match: homicide falls when health coverage expands.

authors: Jessica T. Simes, Jaquelyn L. Jahn
title: The consequences of Medicaid expansion under the Affordable Care Act for police arrests
key_finding: Expanded Medicaid insurance reduced police arrests, particularly drug-related arrests; conclusion supports that broad health policy reforms can meaningfully reduce contact with the criminal justice system.
relevance_to_our_pattern: Covers both the investment lane and the ledger-visibility mechanism: health policy reduces CJ contact, which in turn changes what city vs state ledgers can be counted to do.

authors: Erkmen Giray Aslim, Murat C. Mungan, Carlos I. Navarro
title: The Effect of Public Health Insurance on Criminal Recidivism
venue: Journal of Policy Analysis and Management
key_finding: Public health insurance reduces criminal recidivism; the welfare effect is estimated net of a moral-hazard offset.
relevance_to_our_pattern: Public insurance → less recidivism: behavioral-impulse mechanism.

authors: Kathryn L. Wagner
title: Public Health Insurance and Impacts on Crime Incidences and Mental Health
venue: The B.E. Journal of Economic Analysis & Policy
key_finding: Medicaid expansions for individuals with disabilities produce a short-run reduction in crime, strongest in the years immediately following expansion, plus reduced poor-mental-health days.
relevance_to_our_pattern: Same sign and, importantly for our t+1-lag finding, effect concentrated in immediate post-expansion years.

authors: Steven Mello
title: More COPS, less crime
key_finding: COPS hiring grants causally reduced violent crime ≈4% per officer per 10k residents; grant timing is exogenous to local crime conditions by design.
relevance_to_our_pattern: Template for breaking reverse causation: only exogenous-shock studies of officers/support dollars distinguish policy effect from funding-follows-crisis.

authors: William N. Evans, Emily Greene Owens
title: COPS and crime
key_finding: Using COPS grant allocations for identification, police hiring reduces local crime; magnitude consistent with prior estimates of police productivity.
relevance_to_our_pattern: Establishes a positive causal lane coexisting with our +0.243/+.394 correlational ones; the two classes must be read separately.

authors: Emily Weisburst
title: Safety in Police Numbers: Evidence of Police Effectiveness from Federal COPS Grant Applications
key_finding: Exploits variation in approved vs denied COPS hiring grants; finds police hiring reduces violent crime, while also documenting that grant applications respond to anticipated crime.
relevance_to_our_pattern: Directly documents the funding-follows-crisis channel inside the same literature.

authors: Thomas B. Marvell, Carlisle E. Moody
title: Specification Problems, Police Levels, and Crime Rates
key_finding: Research on police–crime is 'subject to uncertain causal direction and omitted controls'; recommends Granger tests and proxies to separate deterrence from endogeneity.
relevance_to_our_pattern: The classic framing of our officers/100k puzzle (+0.243): positive bivariate slope is endogenous until identification is imposed.

authors: Tomislav V. Kovandzic, John J. Sloan
title: Police levels and crime rates revisited
key_finding: Re-tests police-levels/crime relationship using panel methods; contested deterrence effect with specification sensitivity.
relevance_to_our_pattern: Confirms instability of the raw police-crime slope across specifications.

authors: Aaron J. Chalfin, Justin McCrary
title: Are U.S. Cities Underpoliced? Theory and Evidence
key_finding: Documents measurement error in police data; measurement-error-corrected estimates of police elasticity are similar to quasi-experimental magnitudes; U.S. cities are 'substantially underpoliced'.
relevance_to_our_pattern: Says our +0.243 is likely attenuated by measurement error — but the sign puzzle under reverse causation remains as we flagged.

authors: Steven D. Levitt
title: Understanding Why Crime Fell in the 1990s: Four Factors that Explain the Decline and Six that Do Not
key_finding: Four factors explain the entire 1990s crime drop: more police, bigger prison population, waning crack epidemic, and legalized abortion; 'common explanations' including policing levels measured naively do not suffice.
relevance_to_our_pattern: The benchmark: what counts as a credible driver vs what gets ruled out; our MO-DMH finding must beat this bar.

authors: Andrew F. Henry, James F. Short
title: Suicide and Homicide: Some Economic, Sociological, and Psychological Aspects of Aggression
key_finding: Classic: both homicide and suicide are aggression externalizations whose rates covary; direction (inward vs outward) varies with social/economic position — [hypothesis] from 1950s cross-sectional ecological data.
relevance_to_our_pattern: Original theory of our +0.515: shared aggression pool, structural drivers move both.

authors: Candice Batton
title: Gender differences in lethal violence: Historical trends in the relationship between homicide and suicide rates, 1960–2000
key_finding: Examines historical homicide–suicide rate co-movement through integrated homicide-suicide theory; the relationship is stable but structured by gender and era.
relevance_to_our_pattern: Confirms our +0.515 class of shared-structural-drivers.

authors: Andrew Anglemyer, Hacsi Horvath, George W. Rutherford
title: The Accessibility of Firearms and Risk for Suicide and Homicide Victimization Among Household Members: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
key_finding: Firearm access is associated with elevated risk for both suicide and homicide victimization at the individual level; pooled data confirm co-movement of the two.
relevance_to_our_pattern: Mechanism candidate for shared structural driver: means availability.

authors: Anna E. Austin, Rebecca B. Naumann, Nicole A. Short
title: Association Between Medicaid Expansion and Suicide Mortality Among Nonelderly US Adults
key_finding: Medicaid expansion states had 1.2 fewer suicide deaths per 100,000 per year post-expansion, versus nonexpansion counterfactual.
relevance_to_our_pattern: Bridges MH investment to BOTH violent-death rates: supports our +0.515 co-movement and the investment lane.

authors: Austin et al. (Am J Prev Med)
title: The Evolving Impact of Medicaid Expansion on Suicide Mortality: Demographic and Method-Specific Effects
key_finding: Medicaid expansion was associated with 1.01 fewer suicides per 100,000 nonelderly adults; protective effects grew over time and were largest for ages 18–29.
relevance_to_our_pattern: Time-varying effect matches our t+1-lag strengthening observation.

authors: Devin English, Ty A. Robinson, Lori S. Hoggard
title: Longitudinal Associations From US State/Local Police and Social Service Expenditures to Suicides and Police-Perpetrated Killings Between Black and White Residents
key_finding: Police expenditures predicted increases in suicide and police-perpetrated killings for Black residents; housing/community-development expenditures were associated with decreases in suicide.
relevance_to_our_pattern: Establishes the expenditure-lane literature uses Census-of-Government-style budget lines; supports our state-vs-city ledger split as the right axis.

authors: Seena Fazel, Martin Grann
title: The Population Impact of Severe Mental Illness on Violent Crime
key_finding: Among 98,082 Swedish registry patients with severe mental illness diagnosis, most violent-crime attribution is concentrated in the comorbid substance-abuse subgroup; SMI alone accounts for a small share at the population level.
relevance_to_our_pattern: Bounds the mechanism: MH investment reduces violent crime through targeted treatment, not through broad removal of a large offender pool.

authors: Linda A. Teplin, Gary M. McClelland, Karen M. Abram
title: Crime Victimization in Adults With Severe Mental Illness: Comparison With the National Crime Victimization Survey
key_finding: Since deinstitutionalization, most persons with severe mental illness now live in the community, where they are at great risk for crime victimization; rates far exceed general-population rates.
relevance_to_our_pattern: Reinforces that MH investment reduces harm to the sickest and may shift victimization rates along with offending rates.

authors: Steven P. Raphael, Michael A. Stoll
title: Assessing the Contribution of the Deinstitutionalization of the Mentally Ill to Growth in the U.S. Incarceration Rate
key_finding: 'We find no evidence of transinstitutionalization' — deinstitutionalization is a minor contributor to U.S. incarceration growth.
relevance_to_our_pattern: Against the 'MH beds → crime' story; strengthens our MH-investment (not beds) framing; also shows crime/incarceration and MH budget flows decouple — which is exactly what the merged-city-ledger issue (5) would obscure.

authors: Seth J. Prins
title: Does Transinstitutionalization Explain the Overrepresentation of People with Serious Mental Illnesses in the Criminal Justice System?
key_finding: Tests the transinstitutionalization narrative critically; finds over-representation cannot be explained by a simple bed-to-jail transfer — structural, social, and economic forces drive the co-movement.
relevance_to_our_pattern: Same direction as Raphael & Stoll: MH budget-ledger vs incarceration decoupling, against the naive beds story.

authors: Henry J. Steadman, et al.
title: Prevalence of serious mental illness among jail inmates
key_finding: SCID-based estimates of current serious mental illness among jail admissions run well below survey-based claims; recent-admit jail SMI prevalence ~7-15% (SCID-confirmed) — far below the Treatment-Advocacy-Center-style figures.
relevance_to_our_pattern: Warns against the 'jail is the new asylum' magnitude claim; supports our state-DMH-ledger-not-city-ledger approach (5) as the data source of record.

authors: Daniel W. Webster, Cassandra Kercher Crifasi, Jon S. Vernick
title: Effects of the Repeal of Missouri's Handgun Purchaser Licensing Law on Homicides
key_finding: After Missouri's repeal of its handgun purchaser licensing law in 2007, firearm homicide rates rose significantly relative to synthetic-control counterfactual; the increase concentrated in St Louis and Kansas City.
relevance_to_our_pattern: Context control: our StL murder decline co-occurs with known gun-policy shifts; MO-DMH spend is not the only swing factor in the state.
